title: Conway topograph of the binary form attached to a word
connection: Each word gives SL₂ data γ_w = [[A,p],[t,A*]] and hence binary quadratic forms (e.g. the form fixed by γ_w, discriminant (A+A*)² − 4). The topograph shows values on the Farey tree and the 'river' for indefinite forms.
why: Conway's topograph turns representation questions into tree navigation, and ES might become 'a value p appears on a well at depth 3 with prescribed sign'.
first_step: For p < 500 draw topographs of the forms fixed by γ_w; look for a common location of p and the sign.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0047] Express 4uBC − u − B = p with C fixed as a binary form representation and draw its topograph for p = 409 (a (★)-failure).
repo_evidence: Zagier's windmill is the dihedral symmetry of Conway rivers.
repo_note: Conway river/topograph of windmill examined; topograph of γ_w-fixed forms with p location not drawn.

title: Mock modular / indefinite theta (Zwegers) for the two-sign hyperbola count
connection: Counts of lattice points in hyperbolic regions with sign conditions are coefficients of indefinite theta series. Zwegers completes these to non-holomorphic modular objects. ES₅ counts points on XY = tp+1 in a cone with a character.
why: Indefinite theta series are the natural home of 'divisor counts with sign' (e.g. Hecke's indefinite theta, Andrews–Dyson–Hickerson). Size log²n is consistent with mock objects of weight 1 (σ₀-type).
first_step: For fixed C, write the generating function Σ_{u,B≥1} q^{4CuB−u−B} and test whether it is a known mock theta / Appell–Lerch sum.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0104] Write Σ_n N₋(n) qⁿ as an indefinite theta series of signature (1,1) or (2,2) with a character; check the Zwegers/Vignéras convergence conditions.
repo_note: Mock/Appell–Lerch part examined for a related identity; this two-sign hyperbola count not completed.

title: Rudnev point–plane incidences / Stevens–de Zeeuw in 𝔽_p for modular hyperbola data
connection: Rudnev's point-plane bound and Stevens–de Zeeuw point-line bounds over 𝔽_p give incidence counts beyond trivial; ES Type II solutions are points on modular hyperbolas ff′ ≡ 1 in boxes.
why: Incidence bounds control how many hyperbola points can concentrate, useful for second moments of R(p).
first_step: Count Type II certificate points as incidences between a point set {(f,f′)} and a family of hyperbolas indexed by (c,d) mod p; apply Stevens–de Zeeuw.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0082] Express ES(p) as existence of an incidence between a point set P_p and a line set L_p over F_p (or ℤ) and check sizes vs Rudnev's bound regime.
refs: Stevens–de Zeeuw, An improved point-line incidence bound over arbitrary fields, Bull. LMS 49 (2017), arXiv:1609.06284
Rudnev, On the number of incidences between points and planes in three dimensions, Combinatorica 38 (2018)
repo_note: Incidence/sum-product tools examined for ES (O148(c)); Rudnev/Stevens–de Zeeuw bounds not applied to hyperbola data explicitly.

title: Chevalley–Warning / Ax–Katz over F₂ for a parity count of certificates
connection: Chevalley–Warning gives #solutions ≡ 0 (mod p) for low-degree systems over F_p; integer analogues count solutions mod 2 via polynomial identities. INVOLUTION_ES / WINDMILL ask for an odd weighted count of ES solutions.
why: It is the algebraic native parity tool. It applies to finite-field point counts, not positive integer points, unless the certificate set is encoded as F₂-points of an auxiliary variety.
first_step: Encode the slot-lemma condition (4 | some pentagon entry) as F₂-variety points of an auxiliary system over (ℤ/2)^k (via binary digits?) and compute counts mod 2 for p < 2000.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0085] Find a polynomial system over F_2 or F_3 whose solution set maps onto ES(p) certificates for p ≤ 10³; check CW degree condition.
repo_note: Chevalley–Warning and count-congruence route examined; T1 odd-square barrier noted; integer parity analogue not separately closed.

title: Lattice-point counting in −Γ₁(c) with fixed upper-right entry p (Kloosterman/Kuznetsov for Γ₁(c))
connection: ES₅ ⇔ ∃ c ≥ 2, γ = [[a, p],[c, d]] ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c), a, d in the word range, and (a/p) = −1. So γ ∈ −Γ₁(c)·(unipotent) with fixed b = p. Kuznetsov's formula for Γ₁(c) (with nebentypus) counts such matrices with smooth weights.
why: It gives the precise spectral-theory native form, with the Jacobi twist making it a metaplectic Kuznetsov (Proskurin) problem. B3 says the main term is too small, but the c-sum gives many groups.
first_step: Write the c-summed count as a sum over Γ₁(c) Kloosterman sums S(0, p; c)-type and record the main term size; check with METAPLECTIC_ES.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0088] Formulate R(p) as Σ_{γ ∈ U\Γ/…} with b-entry p and congruence; compute its spectral expansion's main term and check it equals M₀.
repo_note: Bruhat/double-coset and Kuznetsov/θ at fixed p examined (O260); Γ₁(c) Kloosterman lattice count not completed.

title: Bourgain–Gamburd expansion in SL₂(ℤ/q) for ES₅ words
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd (and Bourgain–Varjú for composite q) prove Cayley graphs of SL₂(ℤ/q) w.r.t. Zariski-dense generators are expanders; ES₅ / SL₂-word forms of ES express solutions as length-3 words in a fixed generating set.
why: Expansion gives equidistribution of long words; ES fixes length 3, so the relevant input is the short-word distribution — a known barrier (B3) recorded rather than judged.
first_step: Compute the image of all length-≤3 ES₅ words mod q in SL₂(ℤ/q) for q ≤ 200 and measure how much of the target coset they cover.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0089] For q = small modulus, compute the fraction of SL₂(ℤ/q) hit by ES₅ words with entries ≤ p and compare with random.
refs: Bourgain–Gamburd, Uniform expansion bounds for Cayley graphs of SL2(F_p), Ann. Math. 167 (2008)
Bourgain–Varjú, Expansion in SL_d(Z/qZ), q arbitrary, Invent. Math. 188 (2012)
repo_note: Thin-orbit expansion results (Bourgain–Kontorovich) examined for ES word sets; Bourgain–Gamburd for SL₂(ℤ/q) not applied.

title: Non-congruence classes: polynomial identities valid on Chebotarev classes of non-abelian fields (e.g. 2 a quartic residue)
connection: Mordell–Schinzel rule out polynomial identities on square classes (congruence classes). Classes like 'p = x² + 64y²' (2 is a quartic residue) are Chebotarev classes of non-abelian fields and are not unions of congruence classes, so identities with p-dependent algebraic parameters (e.g. involving x, y with p = x² + 64y²) could cover them.
why: The repo has NONCONG_LIFTS. Native class-field-theory classes give an infinite supply of new 'families' whose parameters are norms (x,y), sidestepping the congruence-class formulation of B1.
first_step: Search for ES identities in parameters (x, y) with p = x² + y² (or x² + 64y²) of bounded degree, e.g. x = f(a,b) with p = a² + b², by polynomial ansatz + solve; test coverage of the hard class.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0098] For p ≡ 1 mod 840, test whether p = N(α) for α in ℤ[ζ_3, 2^{1/3}] (i.e. p = x³-form represented) gives a uniform certificate formula.
repo_note: Kummer fields for 2 a quartic residue examined as non-abelian Frobenius classes; polynomial identities on these classes not decided.

title: Bhargava-style composition on (★) triples (2×2×2 cubes)
connection: Bhargava's cubes give composition laws on binary forms. A (★) triple (u, B, C) with 4uBC − u − B = p might be the data of a 2×2×2 integer cube or a pair of binary forms whose composition carries ES structure.
why: A composition law on certificates would be a new structural tool (descent, closure).
first_step: Search for a cube A(u,B,C,p) with small entries whose Cayley hyperdeterminant or derived forms equal expressions like (4uC−1)(4BC−1) = 4Cp+1.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0100] Write 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) as hyperdeterminant-like expression and check whether it equals Cayley's hyperdeterminant of some cube with entries linear in (x,y,z,n).
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x^2 + ny^2 (1989)

title: Lucas-sequence primitive divisors (Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier) as a source of prime divisors ≡ −1 (mod m)
connection: Primitive prime divisors q of U_m(P,Q) satisfy q ≡ (D/q) (mod m), so q ≡ −1 (mod m) when (D/q) = −1. ES Type II needs a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cp+1. If 4Cp+1 shares a primitive divisor with a suitable U_{4C}, the certificate follows.
why: BHV give existence of primitive divisors for all m > 30, a pointwise rigidity theorem. The question is whether p-dependent Lucas sequences can be tied to 4Cp+1.
first_step: Find a Lucas sequence u_m(p) with index m ~ 4C such that p-tied integers 4Cp+1 contain u_m's primitive divisor; test small cases.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0196] Look for Lucas parameters (P,Q) depending on p with 4Cp+1 | U_{4C}(P,Q)·(small) for some C; test small p by search.

[upgrades-0080] For small D and n = 4C, list primitive divisors q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of u_n and test how often p + m ≡ 0 (mod q) can be arranged (it cannot for fixed p unless q | p + m; compute the induced density).
refs: Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier, Existence of primitive divisors of Lucas and Lehmer numbers (Crelle 2001)
repo_note: Primitive prime divisors of Lucas sequences examined; residue ≡ −1 mod m via primitive divisors not settled.

title: Lee–Yang / stability-preserver view of the window generating polynomial
connection: Lee–Yang (zeros on the unit circle for every ferromagnetic Ising model) and Borcea–Brändén stability preservers prove non-vanishing for every instance via polynomial stability. The window certificate count is a coefficient of Π_i (Σ_{|j|≤a_i} x^{j·g_i}) in the group ring; ask whether a multivariate stable polynomial encodes certificate existence so that stability forces a nonzero coefficient.
why: Stability/interlacing proved 'every instance' theorems where probabilistic arguments only gave typical instances.
first_step: Construct P_p(z) = Σ_{(u,B,C) certificate} z^{u+B+C} for small p and plot zeros; look for regularities.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0326] Write the multivariate polynomial Π_i (1 + z_i + z_i^{-1}) with z_i ↦ characters; examine real-stability of natural specialisations for small examples.
refs: arXiv:1304.4132 (Marcus-Spielman-Srivastava, Interlacing families I: all degrees)
repo_note: Stability/Lee–Yang-type nonvanishing examined in interlacing memo; ES window polynomial case not settled.

title: Chen–Stein Poisson approximation for the ES certificate count
connection: Stein's method bounds total-variation distance of a count to Poisson; if R(p) were approximately Poisson(μ) with μ ≍ log²p, P(R=0) ≈ e^{−μ}.
why: Gives a quantitative heuristic and identifies which dependencies (shared prime factors) break Poisson behaviour.
first_step: Define the model with p uniform in a residue class mod large M; compute Stein–Chen dependency neighbourhoods and TV bound.

title: Coppersmith small-root method: find (d, d′) with dd′ = 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C as a small root of a bivariate polynomial
connection: Writing d = 4Ck − 1 makes the condition (4Ck−1)·d′ = 4Cp+1, a bivariate polynomial with a small root (k, d′). Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham finds small roots when they exist below a size bound.
why: This is the crypto-native 'factoring with a hint' toolbox. A lattice whose reduced basis has a short vector exactly when a certificate exists would be an existence criterion of a new kind (a Minkowski bound).
first_step: Set up f(C,k) = 4uCk − u − k − p and compute the Coppersmith bound X·Y ≤ p^δ for which small roots are guaranteed to be found; compare with expected certificate sizes (C,k ≤ ?).

[signature-0140] Express the ES fixed-C divisor condition as a polynomial congruence and test Coppersmith bounds on p up to a small bit size, comparing against direct divisor enumeration.

title: Divisors of a single integer equidistributing in residue classes (Montgomery/Erdős–Hall for one N)
connection: For one integer N with many prime factors, its divisors equidistribute mod q under mild hypotheses (a Fourier / random-walk argument on (ℤ/q)^×). ES needs this for N = 4Cp+1, which typically has few (~log log p) factors.
why: It is the native single-integer statement. Its failure mode (few prime factors) is exactly why ES is hard; the field has results for 'typical' N only.
first_step: Find a theorem of the form: if τ(N) ≥ q^A and N has no small prime-power obstruction, then divisors of N cover (ℤ/q)^×; check its proof's dependence (it's essentially Davenport-constant).
alt_first_steps: [translate-0084] Quantify: for N with ω(N) = k primes in random classes mod q, P(no divisor ≡ −1) ≈ ? (subset-product random walk). Compare with observed per-level failure.

title: Smooth values of 4Cp+1: certificate abundance when some level is smooth
connection: If 4Cp + 1 has many prime factors whose classes in (ℤ/4C)^× are in general position (smoothness alone is not enough: factors all ≡ 1 mod 4 never give a level-4 certificate), its divisors cover (ℤ/4C)^× (subset products), so a certificate exists. ES would follow from 'for every p some C ≤ (log p)^A has 4Cp + 1 with ≥ k prime factors in general position'.
why: Smooth-number theory (Canfield–Erdős–Pomerance; smooth values of linear forms, Harman; Balog–Wooley) gives existence of smooth values in short families. One value with many factors is a pointwise target with a native toolbox.
first_step: Compute, for hard primes, min over C ≤ 10⁴ of the largest prime factor of 4Cp+1 relative to the requirement Ω ≥ D((ℤ/4C)^×) ; record gap.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0244] Find the best known result on 'some n ≤ N^ε in a linear family an + b has a smooth or many-factor value' (Balog, Harman), and compare the family length (log p)^A with what is needed.
refs: Granville, Smooth numbers: computational number theory and beyond (2008)
repo_note: General-position smooth-level abundance not examined.

title: Titchmarsh divisor problem with congruence: Σ_{p≤x} #{d | p+a : d ≡ r mod q}
connection: Summing ES certificate counts over p is a Titchmarsh-type divisor problem in progressions (Fouvry, Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec). It controls averages and exceptional sets, as LORENZINI_W used Linnik/Halberstam.

title: Divisor function in arithmetic progressions to large moduli (Fouvry–Iwaniec, Heath-Brown τ₃) applied to Σ_C
connection: τ in APs with modulus beyond √x (via Kloosterman, Deshouillers–Iwaniec) ↔ divisors of 4Cp+1 in class mod 4C averaged over C.
why: Average over C at fixed p is a genuine one-variable average (not over p) — exactly the kind of thick average available at a single p. Level-of-distribution results for τ(n) in APs n ≡ a mod q with q ~ n^{2/3} might count Σ_C at fixed p!

So count pairs (d, C) with 4C | d+1 and d | 4Cp+1 — rewrite and see if it reduces to a count of p in residue classes mod d (averaged over d) — Bombieri–Vinogradov at a single p? Check.

title: I3 (n = tuv − u − v, t,u,v ≥ 3) via the hyperbola method + Kloosterman refinement
connection: I3 says every n > 2 433 600 is tuv − u − v with t,u,v ≥ 3; for fixed t, n + (u+v) = tuv ⟺ (tu − 1)(tv − 1) = tn + 1 — a divisor event for tn+1 in the class −1 (mod t).
why: I3 is the same 'divisor of tn+1 ≡ −1 (mod t)' event with a free t — exactly ES's B2 shape but with t ≥ 3 free; the repo's I3 census to 10^9 gives strong data.

title: Random walks on (ℤ/q)^× generated by prime factors: cutoff and mixing of subset products
connection: Subset products of k random elements of an abelian group G cover G once k ≳ log|G| (Erdős–Rényi random subset products). ES wants −1 covered with k ≈ log log p generators: a 'pre-cutoff' regime.
why: Random-walk theory is precise about pre-cutoff probabilities; combined across many levels C it gives a heuristic failure probability.
first_step: Compute P(−1 ∈ subset-products) for k random elements of (ℤ/4C)^× by exact enumeration; plug into a Poisson model over C ≤ C₀.

[tools-0094] Compute the distribution of random subproducts of prime factors of N in (ℤ/e)^× and compare P(−1) with 1/φ(e)·#subproducts.

title: Khinchine flatness theorem for convex pieces of the certificate region
connection: A convex body with no lattice points has bounded lattice width (Khinchine flatness). The hyperbolic certificate region splits into convex pieces, so if ES fails at p, every convex piece is lattice-free and thin in some lattice direction.
why: Flatness-type arguments are the geometry-of-numbers native way to derive structure from emptiness. Here 'thin in a direction' might contradict the known shape of the region.
first_step: For a fixed (u,C) box, the certificate set is a coset of a lattice of determinant ~ uC; apply flatness to decide when a box must contain a coset point (it must if box is large relative to modulus) — computes 'guaranteed' boxes and shows the tied-modulus problem.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0200] Take the region {(X,Y): XY ≈ tp+1, X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (t)} in the lattice of those congruences; compute convex pieces' widths and compare with flatness constants.
repo_note: Khinchine flatness for certificate regions not examined.

title: Character-orthogonality formula: level failure ⇔ Σ_χ χ(−1) ∏_{q^e‖N}(1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e) = 0
connection: #{d | N : d ≡ −1 (mod m)} = φ(m)⁻¹ Σ_{χ mod m} χ(−1) ∏_{q^e‖N} Σ_{j≤e} χ(q)^j. Level failure is the vanishing of this non-negative sum, an identity in the characters' values at N's prime factors.
why: It is the harmonic-analysis native form; the sum is a 'multiplicative energy' quantity. Vanishing requires massive cancellation among characters, which might be impossible when N has a factor in a 'generic' class.
first_step: Characterise exactly when the sum vanishes for ω(N) ≤ 3 (finite group computation); this classifies per-level failure patterns.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0333] For a (★)-failing prime (409), compute these product vectors for C ≤ 20 and look at the structure of the vanishing (which characters contribute negative mass).

title: Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa (Gowers–Green–Manners–Tao) for divisor quotient sets
connection: PFR (Marton) over 𝔽₂ⁿ and torsion-free groups: small doubling ⇒ covered by few cosets of a subgroup; the set of prime factors of N mod e generates the ES quotient set.
why: If the ES quotient set has small doubling it is near a subgroup H, and −1 ∈ Q reduces to −1 ∈ H — a cleaner (parity-like) test.

title: Hypergraph containers for 'certificate-avoiding' factorisation patterns
connection: In the abstract model, a failing p corresponds to an assignment of factorisation patterns to {4Cp+1}_C avoiding every certificate, i.e. an independent set in a certificate hypergraph. The container method (Balogh–Morris–Samotij; Saxton–Thomason) counts independent sets and shows that they lie in few small containers.
why: Containers would give an upper bound on the number of consistent avoiding patterns, which gives exceptional-set bounds via counting, a native extremal-combinatorics route.
first_step: Formalise the hypergraph on (level, residue-class-of-factor) vertices; estimate codegrees and apply the container lemma heuristically to bound the avoiding patterns.
